findings.headline: Statutory service cost pressures growing faster than available funding
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly flags concerns about increased pressures and growing demand in Social Care and Education, with funding failing to keep pace with inflationary, service and demographic pressures. Additional Learning Needs (ALN) demands are increasing in both volume and complexity. The council is setting aside additional reserves to address these pressures, signalling they expect continued strain.
findings.matters: Statutory services (social care and education) must be funded. If costs are growing faster than funding and cannot be constrained, the council faces structural budget pressure that will require further savings or reserve depletion in coming years.
findings.figures: £1.27m set aside to support ALN pressures for 2026/27
findings.quote: This remains a challenging financial period and some specific service issues, along with inflationary pressures across all services, are becoming increasingly hard to finance as our funding fails to keep up with inflationary, service, and demographic pressures.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection shortfall of £939k from rising historic debt
findings.detail: The Council Tax collection shortfall is mainly due to increasing historic Council Tax debt (more than 12 months overdue) requiring higher bad debt provisions. This collection trend is seen across Wales. While in-year collection remains strong at 96.88% (3rd highest in Wales), the historic debt problem represents a structural cash flow and collection issue.
findings.matters: Historic debt buildup indicates weakening collection performance and cash flow pressure. The pattern is not council-specific but systemic across Wales, suggesting potential structural issues in council finances across the region.
findings.figures: £939k shortfall, in-year collection 96.88% (3rd highest in Wales)
findings.quote: there is a shortfall in Council Tax collection of £939k. This is mainly due to an increase in historic Council Tax debt (due more than 12 months ago) and the resulting need to increase our provision for bad debt. This trend has been seen across Wales.

findings.headline: Schools moved to £2.457m deficit despite £5.2m additional council investment
findings.detail: Schools collectively drew down £3.061m from reserves during the year, moving from £604k surplus to £2.457m deficit. The number of schools in deficit rose to 25 from 22 in the previous year. The CFO notes schools are likely to face significant financial challenges in 2026/27 and beyond, reflecting wider national pressures in Wales.
findings.matters: Despite substantial council investment, schools are still drawing down reserves and increasing deficit balances. This indicates fundamental structural pressure in education funding that the council cannot contain, and represents growing financial risk.
findings.figures: £2.457m deficit carried forward (from £604k surplus), £3.061m reserve drawdown, £5.2m additional investment, 25 schools in deficit (up from 22)
findings.quote: The overall schools' balances carried forward into 2026/27 is a deficit of £2.457m, compared with balances brought forward into 2025/26 of £604k, which means schools have collectively drawn down £3.061m resulting in an overall deficit position.

findings.headline: School Balances recovered from £604k deficit to £2.5m positive in one year
findings.detail: School reserves swung from a £604k cumulative deficit at 31 March 2025 to a £2,457k positive balance at 31 March 2026, driven by a £3,061k in-year transfer. This sharp reversal suggests either clawback of previous deficits or a deliberate injection to stabilize school finances.
findings.matters: School deficits are a leading indicator of broader pressure on education budgets; the reversal is positive but the speed and magnitude raises questions about sustainability and whether primary budget pressure merely shifted to the council's account
findings.figures: Moved from (£604k) deficit to £2,457k positive, driven by £3,061k transfer

findings.headline: Coastal Defence capital reserve reached £16.3m and absorbed £2.7m in the year
findings.detail: The Coastal Defence scheme reserve is now the council's largest single capital earmark at £16,308k, having grown from £13,606k with a £2,702k in-year transfer. This multi-year build suggests an ongoing, material capital commitment to coastal protection infrastructure.
findings.matters: A lender assessing long-term financial capacity needs to know the funding certainty and end-date of a commitment this large; if grant-dependent, a withdrawal or reduction poses refinancing risk
findings.figures: £16,308k at 31 March 2026, £2,702k added in-year
findings.quote: Capital Schemes: Coastal Defence (10,539) (3,067) (13,606) (2,702) (16,308)

findings.headline: ALN Reforms reserve reached £2.1m after absorbing £1.3m transfer in a single year
findings.detail: The Additional Learning Needs Reforms reserve grew from £825k to £2,095k in 2025-26, with a transfer of £1,270k. This substantial in-year concentration suggests the council is funding anticipated statutory costs for implementing new special education provision rules.
findings.matters: Large earmarks for statutory demand (especially education) that build faster than planned indicate either unknown cost magnitude or compressed implementation timelines; a lender needs to know if the reserve will prove sufficient
findings.figures: £2,095k total reserve, £1,270k added in-year alone

findings.headline: Denbighshire created a £1.5m Council Tax reserve in 2025-26, with no prior year provision
findings.detail: A new Council Tax reserve of £1,500k appeared in 2025-26 with no previous balance. This large, single-year creation is unusual and suggests the council anticipated or encountered either council tax collection volatility, revaluation impacts, or exemptions/appeals that required a dedicated buffer.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand why council tax income was treated as variable enough to warrant a £1.5m reserve; this could flag either collection problems or structural income uncertainty
findings.figures: £1,500k transfer into new Council Tax reserve in 2025-26

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Coastal defence capital scheme involves approved borrowing with future repayment obligations
findings.detail: The Capital Financing budget includes estimated borrowing costs for a coastal defence scheme. The council has committed to repayment in line with an approved schedule and is setting aside reserves to meet those repayments as they fall due.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing creates future revenue obligations; lenders track councils' aggregate capital commitments and whether reserve levels can sustain repayment schedules.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: the budget includes estimated borrowing costs for the coastal defence scheme; in line with the approved repayment schedule, funds are set aside in reserve to meet future repayments

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Education Service faces £1.27m of ongoing Additional Learning Needs pressures
findings.detail: Education Service pressures in ALN have been partially offset by £785k GwE cost repayment, but the council has set aside £1.27m to reserves explicitly to support ALN pressures going forward. This signals demand-led cost growth requiring ongoing budget support.
findings.matters: Growing ALN demand pressures are a structural cost that will recur; relying on reserves to fund them signals structural underfunding of this area.
findings.quote: Pressures in Additional Learning Needs offset by receipt of repayment of costs from GwE (£785k) and effective use of grants. £1.270m set-aside to reserves to help pressures in Additional Learning Needs

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Headline underspend masks reliance on £3.771m one-off Welsh Government grant
findings.detail: The reported £998k underspend in Corporate & Miscellaneous largely reflects one-time receipt of £3.771m Welsh Government grant for employee costs. The paper does not indicate this funding will recur, meaning the underlying budget position is materially weaker than the outturn headline suggests.
findings.matters: One-off grants mask structural budget gaps; their absence next year would expose whether the council's baseline operations can sustain themselves.
findings.quote: Budget underspend is due to receipt of a Welsh Government grants (£3.771m) to support the Council with additional employee costs

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Highways service failing to deliver £327k of planned savings
findings.detail: Highways reports continuing difficulty achieving £212k of planned savings in Public Conveniences and £115k in structure costs. These delays indicate struggle to implement efficiency measures that were budgeted as part of the council's savings plans.
findings.matters: Consistent failure to deliver budgeted savings signals operational difficulty executing planned efficiency and raises risk on future savings assumptions.
findings.quote: Budget pressure due to continuing process to achieve saving proposals in the Public Conveniences service (£212k), to achieve savings in structure costs (£115k)

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Planning service reporting £623k shortfall in car parking income
findings.detail: The Planning, Public Protection and Countryside service underperformed on car parking revenue expectations by £623k. This was the primary driver of the service's £424k overspend position, only partially offset by underspends in transport and grant income elsewhere in the service.
findings.matters: A material shortfall on a controllable, sustainable revenue stream suggests demand weakness or collection/pricing issues that will persist unless addressed.
findings.quote: Budget pressure from shortfalls in car parking income (£623k) partly offset by underspends in school transport

findings.headline: Council's unearmarked reserves stand at only 2.14% of the net revenue budget, limiting shock absorption
findings.detail: The Council Fund balance is £6.6m, which represents 2.14% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget of £309m. The council acknowledges that "Due to inflation in recent years being at high levels the Council's net revenue budget has increased and the value of the unearmarked reserve, relative to net budget has been eroded" and states it is an aim "to continue to increase the level of un-earmarked reserves over the medium term where possible."
findings.matters: At only 2.14% of budget, the council has minimal buffer for unexpected cost pressures or revenue shortfalls. Any significant adverse event (grant cut, cost overrun) would force either immediate service cuts or drawing on earmarked reserves.
findings.figures: Council Fund balance £6.6m; net revenue budget 2026/27 £309m; unearmarked reserves as % of budget 2.14%
findings.quote: £6.6m is 2.14% of the net revenue budget for 2026/27 at £309m and it is an aim to continue to increase the level of un-earmarked reserves over the medium term where possible.

findings.headline: Children's placements and homelessness costs are rising faster than inflation and are difficult to control
findings.detail: The council identifies Children's Services placements as having demand that is "difficult to forecast" with "complexity of needs coupled with inflation" driving up costs significantly. Welsh Government's priority to eliminate private profit from looked-after children's care is driving costs up in advance of legislative deadlines. For homelessness, a "significant increase in the number of people presenting as homeless in recent years" has led to "significant additional cost, particularly in relation to temporary accommodation." While workstreams aim to reduce costs, "the situation can change quickly."
findings.matters: These are statutory services where demand and cost pressures are largely outside the council's control. Unbudgeted cost escalation in these areas would directly impact the council's ability to balance budgets and would require draw-down of reserves or cuts to other services.
findings.figures: No specific quantum given; identified as an emerging risk with the caveat that homelessness temporary accommodation costs are "significant" and that workstreams show "positive results to reduce the costs"
findings.quote: Children's Services Placements – demand is difficult to forecast, complexity of needs coupled with inflation have driven up costs significantly in recent years. WG have set a priority of eliminating private profit from the care of looked after children, this is having an impact on the market in Wales by driving up costs in advance of those legislative deadlines.

findings.headline: An £11m funding gap remains for 2027/28 even with a 5.9% Council Tax rise; 19% increase would be needed to avoid service cuts
findings.detail: For 2027/28, a mid-range Council Tax increase of 5.9% would yield only £5m and address roughly a third of the funding gap, leaving an £11m shortfall. The council would need to raise Council Tax by 19% to balance the budget without service reductions. No indication of Welsh Government funding levels beyond 2026/27 has been provided.
findings.matters: The council faces difficult and politically constrained choices to close a material gap. A lender needs to understand whether the council has credible plans to close the gap and whether reliance on service cuts or reserves will erode financial resilience.
findings.figures: 2027/28 funding gap £11m; Council Tax increase assumption 5.9% yielding £5m; Council Tax increase required to balance without cuts 19%
findings.quote: A mid-range assumption of a Council Tax increase of 5.9% for 2027/28 yields an additional £5m and addresses roughly a third of the funding gap, the remaining gap is £11m. Council Tax would need to be set at 19% in theory to set a balanced budget with no reductions to budgets.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget pressures of £94m over four years are unprecedented for this council
findings.detail: The council faced £94m in cumulative pressures from 2023/24 to 2026/27, with Welsh Government funding covering only just over half (£51m) and the council forced to find £25m in savings or service reductions. The council explicitly states: 'The Council has not experienced sustained pressures at such a high level before.'
findings.matters: Unprecedented scale of pressures indicates structural stress in the council's financial position and suggests the underlying drivers (demand, pay inflation, service complexity) are not being resolved, only managed year-to-year.
findings.figures: Cumulative pressures £94m; Welsh Government funding £51m; savings/measures £25m; Council Tax increases £18m
findings.quote: The cumulative pressures over the 4-year period from 2023/24 to 2026/27 total £94m. The Council has not experienced sustained pressures at such a high level before.

findings.headline: School reserves have fallen from £5.7m to a projected deficit of £5.2m, with 22 schools in financial deficit
findings.detail: Combined school reserves have deteriorated from £5.7m in 2020/21 to £0.6m in 2024/25, with a forecast deficit of £5.190m by April 2026. The number of schools in financial deficit has risen from 2 in 2021/22 to 22 in 2024/25. The council acknowledges it is "increasingly concerned about the pressure on school finances" and the rate reserves are reducing.
findings.matters: Schools operating with negative reserves cannot sustain operations and signal structural dysfunction in education funding. This constrains the council's ability to support education and its financial stability more broadly.
findings.figures: School reserves: £5.7m (2020/21) → £0.6m (2024/25) → -£5.190m (April 2026 forecast); schools in deficit: 2 (2021/22) → 22 (2024/25)
findings.quote: Combined level of School Reserves (at year end in £m): 5.7, 12.4, 8.9, 3.6, 0.6; Combined use of reserves during the year (in £m): Increase 6.7, 3.5, 5.3, 3; Number of schools in financial deficit: 8, 2, 3, 13, 22

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Chief Executive and Senior Leadership Team were both changed during 2023–2024, introducing execution risk during financial stress
findings.detail: The council underwent significant leadership turnover: the Chief Executive changed recently, the Senior Leadership Team was restructured in 2023 with several senior officers new to post, and the Cabinet was also relatively new when formed in 2022. The council acknowledges this created risk to the council's budget-setting ability during a period when financial stability was already strained.
findings.matters: Leadership churn during financial distress increases the risk of execution failure. A lender needs confidence that leadership has both the experience and institutional knowledge to navigate sustained budget pressures.
findings.figures: CEO change recent; SLT restructure 2023; Cabinet formed 2022
findings.quote: There has been a change in the Council's Chief Executive Officer in recent months which could potentially have increased the Council's risk. The restructure of the Senior Leadership Team in 2023 meant that some Senior Officers were new into post.

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Financial Regulations have not been updated since the finance system change in April 2024
findings.detail: The council implemented a new financial system in April 2024 that replaced all legacy financial IT systems. A review and update of Financial Regulations was planned for late 2025/26 but has not been completed. The Finance Team lacks capacity to do it.
findings.matters: Procedures that do not match the systems they are supposed to govern create control gaps and audit risk. A 16-month delay in completing this after system implementation is a material governance weakness.
findings.figures: Finance system change: April 2024; review still pending as of May 2026 (13 months after implementation)
findings.quote: A new finance system was implemented during April 2024 which replaced all our financial IT systems. Admittedly it has not been possible to complete the regular review and update of Financial Regulations. There has not been the capacity within the Finance Team to complete the review.

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Reserves only recently recovered from a prolonged depletion, and growth depends on one-off Welsh Government funding
findings.detail: Denbighshire's reserve position was negative for years as the council drew them down to cover in-year overspends. Recent growth in 2024/25 and 2025/26 came entirely from additional one-off Welsh Government funding, not from operational improvement or structural balance.
findings.matters: If reserves are recovering only because of one-off funding rather than structural budget balance, they remain vulnerable to the next pressure. A lender needs to know whether the council can actually build sustainable financial strength.
findings.figures: Reserve growth in 2024/25 and 2025/26 from Welsh Government funding only
findings.quote: Reserves have grown modestly during 2024/25 and 2025/26, due to additional in year funding from Welsh Government. Though the trend before that was negative as the Council has had to use reserves to cover in year unplanned overspends.

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget relies on £3m of undelivered savings, with reserves as the backstop if they fail
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget assumes delivery of £3m in savings that have not yet been identified or secured. The council's explicit strategy is to draw on reserves to cover any shortfall if these savings cannot be delivered in-year.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings targets combined with two years of recent overspending mean reserves are the only buffer between budget balance and a formal notice of distress. If reserves are consumed, capacity to absorb any further pressure vanishes.
findings.figures: £3m savings target for 2026/27
findings.quote: 2026/27 budget contains £3m of savings to be realised. Reserves provide a level of mitigation should savings not be deliverable in year

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Denbighshire overspent its budget in both 2022/23 and 2023/24, with corporate underspends masking service overspends
findings.detail: The council recorded overall budget overspends in two consecutive years. Service departments are systematically overspending and being offset by corporate department underspends. This cross-subsidy is a temporary solution that masks underlying service cost control problems.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of overspend indicates systematic control failures or significant underestimation of service costs. When overspends are masked by corporate underspends, flexibility to absorb future pressures is depleted.
findings.figures: Overspends in 2022/23 and 2023/24; service overspends offset by corporate underspends in 2023/24 and 2024/25 (absolute figures not disclosed)
findings.quote: The Council found itself in an overall position of overspending against its budget in 2023/24 and 2022/23. It must be noted that it has been corporate underspends that have been funding service overspending in 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increasing by £9.3m in 2026/27, adding to long-term revenue obligations
findings.detail: The CFR is projected to increase by £9.3m during 2026/27 and remain elevated through 2028/29, reflecting capital spending financed through borrowing that will require repayment from revenue for decades. This growth commits future revenue to servicing debt rather than service delivery.
findings.matters: A growing CFR indicates the council is accumulating long-term debt obligations that constrain future financial flexibility. Each £1m of CFR requires approximately £50-60k annual revenue commitment for repayment and interest.
findings.figures: CFR increase of £9.3m in 2026/27; total CFR projected at £423.7m (2027) rising to £425.4m (2029)
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £9.3m during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council carries £327m debt at 4.7% average cost against investments earning only 3.89%
findings.detail: The council has £327m in borrowing at an average interest rate of 4.7% against only £31.5m in treasury investments earning 3.89%. This 81 basis point unfavorable spread is paid out of the revenue budget annually and represents a structural drag on finances as long as debt exceeds investments.
findings.matters: For a lender, this shows the council carries substantial debt and has minimal liquid reserves to offset it. The unfavorable rate spread indicates the council's historical borrowing has been expensive; if future rates rise, this spread widens further.
findings.figures: £327m borrowing @ 4.7% average; £31.5m treasury investments @ 3.89%; 81 basis point spread
findings.quote: Due to decisions taken in the past, at the time of writing the Council has £327m borrowing at an average interest rate of 4.7% and £31.5m treasury investments at an average rate of 3.89%.

findings.headline: Gross debt is growing faster than the Capital Financing Requirement, halving the council's compliance margin by 2029
findings.detail: Projected debt grows from £360.2m in 2026/27 to £393.4m in 2028/29 while the CFR grows from £423.7m to only £425.4m. The gap between debt and CFR shrinks from £63.5m to £32m—a 50% reduction. Statutory guidance requires debt to remain below CFR; the narrowing margin leaves little room for unexpected borrowing needs.
findings.matters: A narrowing debt-to-CFR ratio indicates the council is approaching its structural debt ceiling. This limits its ability to respond to capital emergencies and suggests future capital spending may be constrained, constraining the council's strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Debt/CFR gap shrinks from £63.5m (2027) to £32m (2029); debt growing £33m while CFR grows only £1.7m
findings.quote: Statutory guidance is that debt should remain below the capital financing requirement, except in the short-term. As can be seen from Table 4, the Council expects to comply with this in the medium-term.

findings.headline: Capital receipts have collapsed, forcing reliance on borrowing to finance capital spend
findings.detail: The council received £3.75m from asset disposals in 2024/25 but has planned only £515k in capital receipts for 2026/27—an 87% decline. With capital receipts now minimal, capital expenditure must be financed entirely from grants, contributions, or new borrowing rather than property sales.
findings.matters: Capital receipts don't require revenue repayment. Their collapse forces the council to borrow more and commit revenue budget to servicing debt for decades, reducing financial flexibility and permanently increasing the cost of capital.
findings.figures: £3.75m capital receipts in 2024/25; £515k planned for council fund in 2026/27 (87% decline)
findings.quote: In 2024/25, £3.75m capital receipts were received from the sale of an agricultural estate, two pieces of land, some Council offices and a former lifeguard factory. A further £0.05m has been received so far in 2025/26. The Council has a programme of potential disposals which is reported to the Asset Management Group.

findings.headline: Nearly one-third of 2026/27 council fund capital is from unapproved estimated new projects
findings.detail: The capital plan includes £15.637m for estimated new projects that have not yet been approved by council. These include block allocations and Sustainable Communities for Learning schools projects. If approved, they will require financing, likely through additional borrowing; if not approved, the forecast is wrong.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the capital program. Material uncertainty about £15.6m of a £47.3m plan affects debt forecasting and reveals whether the council has clear visibility over committed capital.
findings.figures: £15.637m unapproved estimated new projects out of £47.285m total council fund capital (33%)
findings.quote: The estimated new projects include projects which are in the pipeline but have not been approved by Council , such as the block allocations and Sustainable Communities for Learning schools projects.
